title: A 55-Year-Old Math Problem Was Solved—This Time by Humans
gist: Ronald Graham's 1971 rearrangement conjecture, about ordering nonzero numbers in modular arithmetic so that every partial sum is distinct, has been proved for large primes p across four papers by young mathematicians. The last paper, by Lisa Sauermann and Huy Tuan Pham in February 2026, closed the medium-size case using anti-concentration and Fourier analysis. The work shows how randomized constructions and collaboration across subfields can break long-stalled problems.

insights.claim: Graham's rearrangement conjecture was solved by a common strategy: start with a random ordering of the numbers, then repair the few zero-sum intervals that cause repeated partial sums.
insights.speaker: Shalma Wegsman
insights.so_what: 'Random start plus targeted repair' is a general method for search problems where valid solutions are plentiful but hard to state explicitly.
insights.quote: Across the papers, one theme prevailed: the power of randomness to draw out patterns.

insights.claim: Alp Müyesser describes the problem as 'finding the hay in the haystack': good orderings are plentiful, but explicitly describing one is hard, so random constructions succeed where explicit ones fail.
insights.speaker: Alp Müyesser
insights.so_what: Probabilistic existence arguments can beat explicit design in combinatorial problems, a lesson that also applies to algorithm and computer-science research.
insights.quote: If you do it randomly, it’s likely going to work, but it’s hard to explicitly describe what the solution is supposed to look like.

insights.claim: Müyesser and Pokrovskiy handled sets containing almost every number up to p by setting aside a few special spare numbers, randomly shuffling the rest, and inserting a spare wherever an interval summed to zero.
insights.speaker: Shalma Wegsman
insights.so_what: Holding a small reserve to fix the failures of a random process is a reusable design pattern.

insights.claim: Sauermann and Pham proved the medium-size case by using Fourier analysis to show that no single sum of random numbers is especially likely, then showing that the total probability of three kinds of bad events was under 100 percent.
insights.speaker: Shalma Wegsman
insights.so_what: Anti-concentration, a technically demanding method, settled a case that had been explicitly considered intractable with the existing methods.
insights.quote: ultimately showing that the total chance of getting a bad event was less than 100 percent

insights.claim: The Sauermann–Pham 27-page proof showed that a random ordering can be fixed to eliminate bad events at least 90% of the time, not merely that a valid arrangement exists.
insights.speaker: Shalma Wegsman
insights.so_what: A high success rate means the method works as a practical randomized algorithm, not just as an existence proof.
insights.quote: a random ordering could be rearranged to eliminate bad events at least 90% of the time

insights.claim: Kravitz says researchers knew an anti-concentration approach might work but avoided it because the mechanics were so intricate, so the final breakthrough came from willingness to try it, not from a new idea.
insights.speaker: Noah Kravitz
insights.so_what: Some long-stalled problems are blocked by how hard known methods are to carry out, not by missing insight.
insights.quote: we just hadn’t had the guts to actually try it

insights.claim: The 1971 Graham conjecture was resolved over four papers from 2022 to February 2026, each covering a different set size: near-full sets (Müyesser–Pokrovskiy, 2022), tiny sets (Kravitz–Bedert, September 2024), more large sets (a five-author team, August 2025), and medium sets (Sauermann–Pham, 2026).
insights.speaker: Shalma Wegsman
insights.so_what: Hard problems often fall by splitting the problem into regimes, with different methods suited to each.

insights.claim: Noga Alon credits collaboration, the younger generation of mathematicians, and probabilistic methods for solving the conjecture.
insights.speaker: Noga Alon
insights.so_what: Human research networks, not just tools, still drive breakthroughs in pure mathematics.
insights.quote: It’s the power of collaboration, the power of the young generation, the power of probabilistic methods

insights.claim: Müyesser's 2022 solution for large sets went unnoticed because it was buried in a paper about a more general problem, so Kravitz later attacked the conjecture without knowing about it.
insights.speaker: Shalma Wegsman
insights.so_what: Results that are hard to find slow progress, which makes literature discovery valuable to research.
insights.quote: In 2022, they posted their solution, though it was hidden in a paper that focused on applying the same technique to a more general problem.

insights.claim: Kravitz notes that his team combined two areas of combinatorics that rarely collaborate and use completely different techniques.
insights.speaker: Noah Kravitz
insights.so_what: Progress at the edges between fields can come from combining techniques that already exist.
insights.quote: It was a pretty unlikely combination of people

insights.claim: The final breakthrough came from an in-person meeting: Sauermann and Pham heard two talks on failed attempts at a September 2025 conference in Germany and had a plan by the end of a three-day visit in Bonn.
insights.speaker: Shalma Wegsman
insights.so_what: Conferences and in-person collaboration still produce breakthroughs in theoretical work.
insights.quote: By the end of their three-day visit, Sauermann and Pham had a plan for how to crack the case.

insights.claim: The combined proof holds only for very large primes p, on the order of 10 to the 100th power, so the conjecture for all p is technically still unsolved and the result has no use for real juggling routines.
insights.speaker: Shalma Wegsman
insights.so_what: An asymptotic proof can settle the theory while leaving practical, finite cases open.
insights.quote: though no one has calculated its exact value, think along the lines of 10 raised to the 100th power

insights.claim: Alon says the proof confirms that useful structures always exist even inside rigid, finite modular-arithmetic settings, which fits a wider body of results on designs and symmetric structures such as sudoku boards and Latin squares.
insights.speaker: Noga Alon
insights.so_what: The result strengthens a general principle that rigid constraints still leave room for structured solutions.
insights.quote: there are some nice structures that always exist
